sources.entry: 4. What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory - Measures the step in cost per access at each cache boundary and the gap a prefetcher hides.

summary.title: What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory
summary.one_liner: Learn how commodity RAM, CPU caches, NUMA and virtual memory work, and how to write code that uses them well on Linux.
takeaways: Why CPU caches exist: main memory is much slower than the CPU, so caches and access patterns decide performance.
How SRAM and DRAM differ in structure, cost and refresh needs, and how the Northbridge/Southbridge and memory controllers shape bandwidth.
How NUMA systems make remote memory access costlier, and why memory placement matters on multi-socket machines.
Section 6 gives programmer advice on writing code that performs well with caches and memory, with tools covered in section 7.
summary.summary: This long paper by Ulrich Drepper (version 1.0, November 2007) explains the structure of memory subsystems on commodity hardware, focusing on Linux. It covers RAM types (SRAM and DRAM, including refresh and leakage), the Northbridge/Southbridge chipset layout, memory controllers, DMA, and NUMA systems. The central section gives programmers advice on writing code that uses CPU caches and memory well, and a later section introduces profiling tools. The text is explanatory, with diagrams and formulas, and uses qualifiers throughout because the technology varies widely. The listing notes a point about the cost step at each cache boundary and prefetching, but the portion of the text provided here ends before the cache and prefetch sections.
